lesson.title: Why the Wall Outlet Never Sits Still: Alternating Current
lesson.summary: Alternating current is electric current whose magnitude and direction reverse in a repeating sinusoidal pattern, and its waveform, frequency, and RMS value are the foundation for every AC concept that follows.
lesson.body:
Direct current flows in one steady direction, like water through a pipe under constant pressure. Alternating current, or AC, is different: its magnitude rises and falls and its direction reverses on a regular, repeating schedule. In nearly every practical power system, that repetition follows a sine wave, so we write the instantaneous current as i(t) = Im sin(wt + theta), where Im is the peak amplitude, w is the angular frequency, and theta is a phase offset. This is exactly the sinusoidal waveform you have already met, now attached to the physical quantity of current, the rate of charge flow past a point in a circuit.

AC did not win out over DC by accident. The decisive advantage is that transformers, which step voltage up or down using electromagnetic induction, only work when the current producing the magnetic flux is changing. Faraday's law says an induced voltage depends on the rate of change of flux, so a constant DC current induces nothing in a nearby coil. By generating power as AC, utilities can raise transmission voltage to hundreds of kilovolts, which shrinks the current needed for a given amount of power and cuts resistive losses, which scale with the square of current, dramatically, then transform the voltage back down to a safe level near your home.

Two numbers describe how fast an AC waveform repeats: the period T, the time for one full cycle, and the frequency f = 1/T, the number of cycles per second, measured in hertz. The angular frequency w = 2*pi*f converts cycles per second into radians per second, which is the natural unit for the sine function. Because a sinusoid spends time at every value between its positive and negative peaks, we rarely quote AC voltage or current by their peak value. Instead we use the root mean square, or RMS, value: Vrms = Vm / sqrt(2) for a pure sinusoid. RMS is defined so that an AC source with that RMS value delivers exactly the same average power to a resistor as a DC source of the same numeric value.

Consider a standard North American wall outlet, rated at 120 V and 60 Hz. That 120 V is an RMS figure, so the actual peak voltage is higher: Vm = Vrms times sqrt(2) = 120 times 1.4142, about 169.7 V. The period is T = 1/f = 1/60, about 16.7 milliseconds, and the angular frequency is w = 2*pi(60), about 377 rad/s. Suppose you want the instantaneous voltage 5 milliseconds after the waveform crosses zero going positive. Plugging in, wt = 377 times 0.005, about 1.885 radians, which is about 108.0 degrees, and sin(108.0 degrees) is about 0.951. So v(0.005 s) is about 169.7 times 0.951, roughly 161.4 V, meaning the outlet is already past its peak and coming back down at that instant, even though it never actually reaches a stable value the way a battery does.

Because AC is constantly changing, two AC waveforms of the same frequency can be offset from each other in time, a relationship we describe with a phase angle. When current and voltage in a circuit are not perfectly in step, something more than plain resistance is at work, energy is being temporarily stored and returned by inductors or capacitors rather than only consumed. Capturing that phase relationship compactly is exactly the problem that impedance, admittance, and phasor analysis are built to solve, and alternating current is the physical signal all of that machinery exists to describe.
